lesson.title: Two Steps, One Pulse: Understanding Pulse Response
lesson.summary: Pulse response describes how an RL or RC circuit reacts to a source that turns on for a limited duration and then turns back off, and it is found by treating the pulse as two separate step responses stitched together at the moment the source switches back off.
lesson.body:
A pulse is a source that jumps up to some value, holds for a finite width, and then drops back down, unlike a step, which jumps once and stays there forever. Digital data bits, camera flash triggers, and relay actuation signals are all pulses rather than pure steps, so understanding how an RC or RL circuit responds to a pulse matters just as much as understanding the step response it is built from. The key insight is that a pulse response is not a new kind of math at all, it is just the step response applied twice: once for the rising edge, and once for the falling edge, using whatever voltage or current the circuit had reached at the moment the source switched back off as the new initial condition for the second stretch.

Reuse the series RC circuit from the step response discussion: R = 3 kilo-ohms, C = 2 microfarads, tau = RC = 6 ms, and a 9 V source. This time, instead of staying on forever, the source is a pulse that turns on at t = 0 and turns back off at t = 6 ms, exactly one time constant later, with the capacitor starting fully discharged. For the interval 0 <= t < 6 ms, the circuit behaves exactly like the step response worked out earlier: v(t) = 9(1 - e^(-t/0.006)) volts. At the instant the pulse ends, t = 6 ms, that formula gives v = 9 x (1 - e^-1) = 9 x 0.6321 = 5.689 V. Because the pulse was only one time constant wide, the capacitor never gets close to the full 9 V; it only reaches 5.689 V before the source disappears.

That 5.689 V becomes the new initial condition for the second phase. Once the source drops to 0 V at t = 6 ms, the capacitor has nothing left to charge toward, so its forced response is now 0 V, and it discharges back down through the same 3 kilo-ohm resistor with the same time constant, tau = 6 ms. Measuring a new local time variable t' = t - 6 ms for convenience, the discharge is v(t') = 5.689 x e^(-t'/0.006) volts for t' >= 0.

Checking that discharge: at t' = 6 ms (t = 12 ms overall, one time constant into the discharge), v = 5.689 x e^-1 = 5.689 x 0.3679 = 2.093 V. At t' = 12 ms (t = 18 ms overall, two time constants into the discharge), v = 5.689 x e^-2 = 5.689 x 0.1353 = 0.770 V. The capacitor never actually reached the source voltage during the pulse and now decays back toward zero rather than continuing to climb, which is the hallmark of a pulse that is narrow relative to the circuit's time constant.

Contrast this with what would happen if the pulse were wide instead, say 30 ms, five full time constants. The capacitor would climb to essentially the full 9 V by the end of the pulse (9 x (1 - e^-5) = 9 x 0.9933 = 8.940 V) before dropping back off, producing a response that looks almost like a flat-topped step rather than the rounded, incomplete bump seen with the 6 ms pulse. Comparing narrow and wide pulses this way is a fast way to judge, just from the ratio of pulse width to tau, whether a circuit will register a clean replica of the input pulse or smear it into something barely resembling the original shape, which matters enormously in digital and communication circuits trying to pass pulses through RC-like wiring without distorting them.

This stitching technique, step up then step down, generalizes to any pulse width and to trains of multiple pulses, and it is the same superposition idea that underlies more advanced signal analysis later on: complicated waveforms get broken into simple steps, each step response is solved on its own, and the pieces are added together respecting when each one starts.
